newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO ponders how long new Bosnia force should stay.
newsitem.headline: NATO ponders how long new Bosnia force should stay.

text.p: NATO countries, having agreed that an alliance-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) should stay in Bosnia next year, are now faced with the question of how long the mission should last.
Officials said on Wednesday that ambassadors from the 16- nation North Atlantic Treaty Organisation had turned to the details of their peace plan for Bosnia, from its mandate to its duration.

No decisions were taken, but the alliance is under some pressure to get their operational plan together in time to have it approved before the mandate of NATO's current Implementation Force (IFOR) in Bosnia expires a month from now on December 20.

NATO agreed in principle on Monday to leave between 25,000 and 30,000 troops in Bosnia next year, with a slightly changed mandate to help civilian institutions develop rather than just enforce the Dayton peace accord.
A key factor behind decisions was the United States's announcement last week that it was prepared to commit 8,500 troops to the new force.
Washington also proposed that the force remain in Bosnia until June 1998 with reviews of its purpose every six months.
Officials said most other NATO countries had been considering keeping a force in Bosnia for just one year, although some, such as France, wanted a two-year mandate.

Germany, which has offered to send 3,000 troops to Bosnia under French command, has not ruled out staying more than a year but said it will only ask the German parliament to approve a one-year deployment.
"Every delegation has its own ideas on this," one NATO official said after a meeting of ambassadors on Wednesday. "Our initial assumption was that (it) would last for one year."
Officials said, however, that there was plenty of room for an agreement to be reached and that alliance members were in broad agreement on a number of major issues concerning the force.
"There is going to be a continual review. Our aim is to have not one soldier in Bosnia at any given time more than necessary," one said. "We are not going to stay 18 months if it is not necessary."
The official also said that the ambassadors had informally agreed that the NATO-led force would be used to support municipal elections which are expected to be held in mid year.
Washington's proposal had also forced NATO to consider when and how to reduce the 30,000-odd SFOR over the period of its mandate.
The United States has called for a sharp reduction at a set point in the 18-month period. Other NATO countries, however, favour a gradual reduction, the official said.

On the military level, the official said, General George Joulwan, the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, was beginningg consultations with national capitals to see how many forces would be committed. He was expected to have his operational plan ready by December 6.
